The branch issue has a workable local treatment: all roots merging at one exterior point must use a compatible logarithm, and changes between branch charts must be retained explicitly. I’m testing a damped Cauchy contour whose vertical tails can be bounded without assuming continuation beyond the known half-plane.

The input audit confirms the inherited formulas and their limits. The symmetry calculation also gives an exact negative-axis branch correction. This supports local conjugation identities and contour folding, but supplies no sign estimate. The draft time-law proof covers the complete divisor locally through exterior mergers and gives explicit bounds for the omitted tails. I’m keeping that analytic result separate from the signed estimate, where the equally informed direct method remains the benchmark.

The contour formula now has explicit bounds for both the divisor cutoff and the vertical tails, with both vertical lines retained. I also checked related superzeta literature; the inspected formulas do not directly supply a theorem for this moving, heat-evolved exterior divisor. The next check is whether the full contour estimate improves the signed bound.

A separate internal reviewer is checking the completed proofs. The cutoff analysis has an important consequence: evaluating the signed residues before taking absolute values gives the sharper divisor remainder. The quantitative comparison will use that sharper bound on both sides.

For the signed-bound test, I’ll use the existing modified-divisor control as a comparator. It can test what follows from the slice estimates and symmetry alone; it does not test the full canonical heat evolution. That distinction will determine the scope of any negative conclusion.

This concerns the modified static-divisor class only; the canonical heat evolution remains open.

How does the complex power time evolution look? What are some of the most relevant formulas for the work so far?
I’ll pull the formulas from the assessed notes and explain how the complex-power evolution connects to the interaction and gap equations.

The key feature is that the evolution retains a term involving \((H_z/H)^2\). At integer powers, this recovers the interaction equation and exposes the extra spatial moment \(T_2^2\); the complex-\(p\) contour then reconstructs the forcing from \(Z(2)\) and \(Z(3)\).

The complex-power evolution is an **exact contour equation for the complete exterior power sum**. Its central feature is a quadratic term in the full spatial logarithmic derivative \(H_z/H\). That spatial information remains essential in the formulas established so far.

Let the selected pair be \(c(t)\pm\sqrt{D(t)}\), and write
\[
w_j=\rho_j-c,\qquad a_j=w_j^2-D,\qquad \ell=\frac1{\log T}.
\]
Here \(\ell\) is fixed in time, and the exterior sum excludes the selected pair but counts every other zero with multiplicity. Define
\[
\boxed{
S(p,t)=\sum_j e^{-p\Log a_j(t)},\qquad
Z(p,t)=\ell^{2p}S(p,t).
}
\]
These sums are holomorphic for \(\Re p>\tfrac12\). Noninteger powers use local analytic logarithm choices; at positive integers,
\[
Z(n,t)=\ell^{2n}S_n(t)
\]
is independent of those choices.

The most useful evolution formula comes from setting
\[
Q=w^2-D(t),\qquad
f_p=\ell^{2p}e^{-p\Log Q},\qquad
h(t,w)=\frac{H_z(t,c(t)+w)}{H(t,c(t)+w)}.
\]
Let \(\mathcal C[g]\) denote the normalized spatial contour integral
\((2\pi i)^{-1}\int g\,dw\), summed over the exterior cluster contours and complete tail boundaries. Then
\[
Z(p,t)=\mathcal C[f_ph].
\]
The centered heat equation gives
\[
h_t=-h_{ww}-2hh_w+c'h_w,
\]
and integration by parts yields
\[
\boxed{
\partial_t Z(p,t)
=
\mathcal C\!\left[
\big((f_p)_t-(f_p)_{ww}-c'(f_p)_w\big)h
+(f_p)_w h^2
\right].
}
\]

Written explicitly in \(p\), this is
\[
\boxed{
\partial_t Z
=
\mathcal C\!\left[
f_p\left\{
\left(
\frac{p(D'+2)}{Q}
+\frac{2pc'w}{Q}
-\frac{4p(p+1)w^2}{Q^2}
\right)h
-\frac{2pw}{Q}h^2
\right\}
\right].
}
\]
All derivatives here use physical time \(t\), holding \(w\) fixed inside the integrand. The complete contour treatment makes this valid locally through exterior zero mergers, without differentiating individual root labels. The result retains \(h^2\); it does not establish an autonomous scalar equation involving only \(Z(p,t)\). [Time-law proof, equations (11)–(18)](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/notes/03_VCD_GT_CM_E02_COMPLEX_POWER_TIME_LAW_20261117.md).

At integer powers, two particularly informative specializations are
\[
\boxed{
M'=2M^2-12S_2-16DS_3,\qquad
D'=2-4MD,\qquad M=S_1.
}
\]
The next moment satisfies
\[
\boxed{
S_2'
=
8MS_2-32S_3+4DS_2^2-40DS_4+4T_2^2,
\qquad
T_2=\sum_j\frac{w_j}{(w_j^2-D)^2}.
}
\]
The \(T_2^2\) term makes the retained spatial dependence visible: the evolution involves the displacements \(w_j\), as well as their squared denominators.

For the gap-transport application, the natural scaling is
\[
m=\ell^2M,\qquad \delta=\frac{D}{\ell^2},
\qquad \sigma=\frac{t-t_0}{\ell^2}.
\]
The equations become
\[
\boxed{
m_\sigma=2m^2-F,\qquad
\delta_\sigma=2-4m\delta,\qquad
F=12Z(2)+16\delta Z(3).
}
\]
Thus the quantitative task is to control the **real signed forcing \(F\)** over the interval.

The complex-\(p\) representation reconstructs precisely that forcing. For fixed \(\epsilon>0\), set
\[
K_\epsilon(p,\delta)
=
\frac{12e^{\epsilon(p-2)^2}}{p-2}
+
\frac{16\delta e^{\epsilon(p-3)^2}}{p-3}.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
F(t)=
\frac1{2\pi i}
\left(
\int_{4-i\infty}^{4+i\infty}
-
\int_{1-i\infty}^{1+i\infty}
\right)
K_\epsilon(p,\delta(t))Z(p,t)\,dp.
}
\]
Both lines run upward, and both remain part of the formula. The damping equals one at the residues \(p=2,3\), while along vertical lines it contributes Gaussian decay \(e^{-\epsilon(\Im p)^2}\). This pays the exponential branch growth and makes the complete integrals converge. [Contour proof, equation (7)](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/notes/05_VCD_GT_CM_E03_DAMPED_CAUCHY_EVOLUTION_20261117.md).

The relevant symmetry is Schwarz conjugation:
\[
\boxed{Z(\bar p,t)=\overline{Z(p,t)}}
\]
when conjugate spatial clusters receive conjugate logarithms. It makes \(Z(p,t)\) real for real \(p\), without determining its sign. If instead every negative-real \(a_j\) receives argument \(+\pi\), the exact fixed-time defect is
\[
Z_+(p)-\overline{Z_+(\bar p)}
=
-2i\,\ell^{2p}\sin(\pi p)
\sum_{a_j<0}|a_j|^{-p}.
\]
The defect vanishes at integer powers. [Symmetry and branch-defect proof](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/notes/04_VCD_GT_CM_E08_CONJUGATION_AND_BRANCH_DEFECT_20261117.md).

Finally, the formula connecting all of this to the actual gap is
\[
\boxed{
W(x,y)\delta(x)
=
\delta(y)-2\int_x^y W(u,y)\,du,
\qquad
W(x,y)=\exp\!\left(-4\int_x^y m(u)\,du\right).
}
\]
A useful forcing bound controls \(m\), hence this transport cost. An independent gap value and an independently justified tube remain necessary.

The present gain is the complete time law, branch accounting, and justified contour limits. The signed estimate remains at the inherited \(O(\log T)\) allowance for fixed collar parameters. Convergence and conjugation alone have not improved it—the distinction recorded in the [result summary](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/result-summaries/18_tensor_approximation_and_coefficient_bounds.md) and [comparison lesson](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/avoid/12_term_by_term_matching_and_separate_bounds.md).
For T_2, can't you subtract and add \sum_j D/(w_j^2-D)^2 to get T_2 = M + DS_2?
I’ll check the recorded definition—the distinction is whether the numerator is \(w_j\) or \(w_j^2\).

Your manipulation works for a **\(w_j^2\) numerator**:
\[
\sum_j\frac{w_j^2}{(w_j^2-D)^2}
=
\sum_j\frac{(w_j^2-D)+D}{(w_j^2-D)^2}
=
\boxed{M+DS_2}.
\]

But the moment appearing in the evolution is defined with a **\(w_j\) numerator**:
\[
\boxed{T_2=\sum_j\frac{w_j}{(w_j^2-D)^2}.}
\]
The subscript \(2\) denotes the denominator power.

Moreover, the evolution contains the square of that entire sum,
\[
T_2^2=\left(\sum_j\frac{w_j}{(w_j^2-D)^2}\right)^2,
\]
which is also different from your squared-numerator sum.

For example, a symmetric pair \(w=\pm r\) contributes zero to \(T_2\), but contributes \(2r^2/(r^2-D)^2\) to \(M+DS_2\).

Oh, right yes I didn't do that carefully. How about noting that w_j^2-D = (w_j+\sqrt{D})(w_j-\sqrt{D}), and doing the same trick, ending with the term \sum_j D/((w_j+\sqrt{D})(w_j-\sqrt{D})^2). You could actually add and subtract or the opposite. That suggests considering a sum with separate powers of w_j-\sqrt{D} and w_j + \sqrt{D}. It might be worth checking if that would close for the evolution equation, at least on integers.
I’ll check the integer hierarchy with separate powers at the two target zeros, including whether its evolution closes and how it behaves when the targets merge.

The algebra is pointing to an infinite integer hierarchy that closes. The separate-pole sums recover the missing odd moments, and those odd moments appear to evolve using the same enlarged family. I’m checking the complete-zero-sum limit and the target-merger case before treating that as established.

The candidate new equation is
\[
T_2'=(6M+8DS_2)T_2-20T_3-40DT_4.
\]
It uses only the enlarged moment family. The calculation also suggests that keeping the even moments \(S_n\) and odd moments \(T_n\) avoids the square-root singularity that individual split-pole sums can develop at \(D=0\).

Every mixed integer sum reduces algebraically to the two sequences \(S_n\) and \(T_n\). The midpoint drift cancels from their evolution, so the closure concerns the relative moments and \(D\). It still uses infinitely many moments; a finite truncation is a separate question.

Both derivations now agree, including the new \(T_2\) equation and the equations for every integer order. An exact quartic heat-flow example checks them through simultaneous target and exterior mergers. A separate reviewer is checking the proof and the passage to the complete canonical divisor.

The reviewer has found no mathematical correction so far. The scope is important: each equation uses finitely many moments from the same infinite family, but higher orders keep appearing. The \(S_n,T_n,D\) formulas remain regular at a merger; they do not by themselves give a finite truncation or a stronger signed bound.

The assessment is complete and accepts the integer closure proofs within their stated domains. Your proposed enlargement works. I’m saving the general recurrences, the merger qualifications, and the updated progress record.

**Yes. Your proposed enlargement gives a closed infinite integer hierarchy**, and it has an equivalent formulation that remains regular when \(D=0\).

Write \(s=\sqrt D\), \(Q_j=w_j^2-D\), and
\[
P_{p,q}=\sum_j\frac1{(w_j-s)^p(w_j+s)^q},
\qquad p,q\ge0,\quad p+q\ge2.
\]
The exact starting identities are
\[
T_2=P_{1,2}+sP_{2,2}
   =P_{2,1}-sP_{2,2}
   =\frac{P_{1,2}+P_{2,1}}2.
\]
Thus the coefficient in this add/subtract step is \(s=\sqrt D\).

The mixed sums recover precisely the missing odd moments. In fact, two sequences suffice:
\[
S_n=\sum_jQ_j^{-n}=P_{n,n},\qquad n\ge1,
\]
\[
T_n=\sum_jw_jQ_j^{-n}
=\frac{P_{n-1,n}+P_{n,n-1}}2,\qquad n\ge2.
\]
Conversely, every permitted \(P_{p,q}\) reduces to a finite combination of these: put it over \(Q^{\max(p,q)}\), expand its polynomial numerator, and use \(w^2=Q+D\).

With primes denoting physical time, the general equations are
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
S_n'={}&2n\sum_{r=1}^{n}S_rS_{n+1-r}\\
&+2n\sum_{r=2}^{n}
 \left(T_rT_{n+2-r}+D S_rS_{n+2-r}\right)\\
&-4n(n+2)S_{n+1}-4n(n+3)D S_{n+2},
\qquad n\ge1,
\end{aligned}}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
T_n'={}&2(2n-1)\sum_{r=2}^{n}T_rS_{n+1-r}\\
&+4nD\sum_{r=2}^{n}T_rS_{n+2-r}\\
&-4(n^2+n-1)T_{n+1}-4n(n+3)D T_{n+2},
\qquad n\ge2.
\end{aligned}}
\]
Empty sums are zero, and
\[
D'=2-4DS_1.
\]

In particular, the previously missing evolution equation is
\[
\boxed{T_2'=(6M+8DS_2)T_2-20T_3-40DT_4.}
\]
So differentiating \(T_2\) introduces higher moments **of the same enlarged family**.

The derivation cancels the potentially nonabsolutely convergent first-power sums before passing to the complete canonical divisor. Under the existing tube and collar hypotheses, the \(S/T\) equations also extend through target and exterior mergers. Individual unsymmetrized \(P_{p,q}\) can have square-root time behavior at \(D=0\); the \(S/T\) formulation avoids that coordinate singularity.

This establishes componentwise **infinite** closure. Higher orders keep appearing, so it supplies neither a finite truncation nor a stronger signed forcing estimate by itself.
